belief: I must hold on to everything.
origins: When money, food, or comfort were scarce, holding on tightly was how a family survived. Saving everything, never wasting, and never letting go can feel like the only safe way. A person may also have been shamed for spending or giving, or may have lived through a loss that taught them to guard what is left.
teaches: Scripture honors saving, planning, and care for what we own. It also warns that life does not consist in the abundance of possessions, and that gripping what we have can crowd out trust. God tells us to be generous and to put our hope in Him, not in uncertain wealth. Giving does not mean being careless; it means holding things with an open hand, trusting that God is our source and that generosity is part of how He refreshes us.
self_statements: If I let go of anything, I will regret it.
Throwing things out is wasteful and dangerous.
I cannot give; I need everything I have.
If I hold on tight enough, I will stay safe.
errors: Predicting that I will need exactly what I let go.
Treating letting go of a small thing as a threat to survival.
Believing that I must keep everything or risk losing everything.
Feeling anxious when I let go and concluding that it is dangerous.
questions: What am I afraid will happen if I let something go?
How often have I actually needed an item I kept “just in case”?
What has holding on cost me in space, peace, or relationships?
What did I learn early in life about keeping and losing?
Where does Scripture connect trust with open hands?
What is one small thing I could release or share this week?
What would I tell a friend who felt this way?
truth: Saving and caring for what I have is wise. But I do not have to hold on to everything to be safe. My security comes from God, not from what I keep. I can hold things with an open hand, share when I am able, and let go of what I do not need.
hw_truths: My safety comes from God, not from what I keep.
I can save wisely and still let go.
Giving can bring peace, not only loss.
I do not need to keep everything “just in case.”
Letting go of small things is a safe practice.
An open hand is not a careless hand.
log: What I kept and what I released
Record one thing you let go of or shared, your fear before from 0 to 10, and what actually happened.
actions: Choose something you have not used in a year. Predict how upsetting it will be from 0 to 10, let it go, and record what happened.
Give a small amount of time, food, or money. Notice the fear and what you feel afterward.
Decide in advance what is worth keeping, such as important papers or sentimental items, so the rest is easier to release.
Hold your hands open for one minute and thank God that He is your source.
prayer: Father, You know why I hold so tightly. Teach me to trust You as my provider. Help me keep what is wise, release what I do not need, and give with an open hand. Amen.
